title: How do you add distributed tracing to a gRPC microservice (client/server interceptors injecting/extracting trace context, Jaeger/Zipkin/OpenTelemetry)?
shortTitle: How do you add distributed tracing to a gRPC microservice (client/server interceptors injecting/extracting trace context, Jaeger/Zipkin/OpenTelemetry)?
keyPoints: A trace follows one request across services as a tree of spans identified by a shared trace ID.
A client interceptor injects the active trace context (trace ID, span ID, sampling flags) into gRPC metadata before each call.
A server interceptor extracts trace context from incoming metadata and starts a child span for the handler.
OpenTelemetry handles inject and extract through its propagators using the W3C traceparent format.
OpenTelemetry ships ready-made gRPC instrumentation so you rarely hand-write interceptors.
Never put sensitive PII like account numbers or balances into span attributes in a banking system.

s1_definition.oneliner: Use a client interceptor to inject trace context into gRPC metadata and a server interceptor to extract it and start a child span, with OpenTelemetry propagating the trace and Jaeger or Zipkin visualizing it.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Distributed trace** – follows a single request across multiple services as a tree of spans under one trace ID.
- **Client interceptor** – injects the current trace context (trace ID, span ID, sampling flags) into gRPC call metadata before sending.
- **Server interceptor** – extracts trace context from incoming metadata and starts a child span, continuing the trace.
- **OpenTelemetry** – the standard instrumentation framework; handles inject and extract through propagators using W3C `traceparent` format.
- **Jaeger/Zipkin** – backends that store and visualize the collected traces as timelines.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a transfer request at National Bank of India passing through several departments. Distributed tracing attaches one tracking number to Rajesh's request and stamps a timestamped slip at every department entry and exit. The client interceptor writes the tracking number on the envelope before sending. The server interceptor reads that number and keeps using it. Jaeger assembles all stamps into one timeline so you see exactly which department was slow.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Transfer Request Flow with Tracing:

  Client App
       │
       │ [trace_id=abc, span_id=001]
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  Transfer Service     │  span: transfer (root)
  │  Client Interceptor:  │
  │  inject(context,      │
  │         metadata)     │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │ gRPC call + metadata [traceparent: abc-001]
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  Account Service      │  span: getBalance (child of abc-001)
  │  Server Interceptor:  │
  │  extract(metadata)    │
  │  startSpan(child)     │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  Ledger Database      │  span: query (child)
  └──────────────────────┘

  Jaeger UI shows:
  trace abc ──▶ transfer(150ms) ──▶ getBalance(80ms) ──▶ query(30ms)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Distributed tracing follows one request across services by recording a tree of spans under a single trace ID. In gRPC, a client interceptor injects the active trace context into the call's metadata, and a server interceptor extracts that context and starts a child span. OpenTelemetry handles inject and extract using the W3C `traceparent` format, and it ships ready-made gRPC instrumentation so you rarely write interceptors by hand.

The exporter sends spans to a backend like Jaeger or Zipkin, and the sampler controls how many traces are recorded. In production, batch the span exports and choose a sampling rate that balances cost against diagnostic coverage.

At National Bank of India, Rajesh's transfer request starts a root span in the transfer service. When the service calls the account service, the client interceptor injects the trace context into the gRPC metadata, and the account service's server interceptor extracts it and starts a child span. In Jaeger, the whole flow appears as one trace with nested spans and timings, so when a transfer is slow, Pankaj sees exactly which hop is responsible.

The senior points are to propagate context correctly across async boundaries, to never put PII into span attributes in banking, and to inject the trace ID into the logging MDC so every log line links to its trace.

Remember one sentence: a client interceptor injects trace context into gRPC metadata, a server interceptor extracts it and opens a child span, and OpenTelemetry propagates the trace end-to-end for fast diagnosis.
